passage: The phone-repair shop near the Nandgaon bus stand had one computer, and the owner's nephew, Bhola, swore it could write anything. "Type 'essay on groundwater, Class 10', Ramesh, and in one minute it's done. Neat English. Madam will never know." Ramesh watched the cursor blink. His own draft sat folded in his pocket: two pages in pencil, full of crossings-out, about the dry well behind his grandfather's field. Vidya, buying a recharge at the counter, glanced over. "Madam asked what we saw in our own village," she said. "Will the machine know your well?" Ramesh thought of the rope marks on the stone, of Dada measuring how far the bucket dropped each summer. The machine would give him perfect sentences about somebody else's water. "Leave it," he told Bhola. That night he copied his pencil draft out neatly and added Dada's summer measurements at the end.

qa.q: What was Ramesh's own draft about?
qa.a: The dry well behind his grandfather's field.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling as he watched the cursor blink?
qa.a: Ramesh felt tempted but uneasy; the neat essay was one click away while his own messy draft sat in his pocket, and Vidya's question tipped him towards pride in his real work.

qa.q: What small step would help Ramesh the next time a shortcut is offered?
qa.a: Ramesh could ask what the teacher actually wants to see, as Vidya did, and remember that details like Dada's measurements are what make the work his own.

qa.q: How might Vidya see Ramesh's choice?
qa.a: Vidya would likely respect it; her question was only a nudge, and he chose his own observations over neat borrowed sentences.

grounding: A small-town teenager turns down a machine-written essay and hands in his own observations of the village well.

passage: Sunday night in Johannesburg, and Dalia's history essay was due at eight the next morning. Her cousin Thabo, a year ahead, slid a folder across the kitchen table. "Same question last year. I got a distinction. Change a few words and go to sleep." Dalia opened it. Clean paragraphs about the city's early gold mines, quotes she would never have found. Her chest loosened, then tightened. If she handed this in and got praised, the praise would belong to Thabo. And in June there would be an exam, no folder allowed. She closed it. "Can you just show me how you found the sources?" Thabo shrugged, a little stung, then pulled up a chair. They worked until eleven. Her essay came out plainer than his, with one argument she was sure was her own.

qa.q: When was Dalia's history essay due?
qa.a: At eight the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Dalia's chest loosen and then tighten when she opened the folder?
qa.a: Dalia felt relieved at first that the work was done, then uneasy, because any praise would belong to Thabo and the June exam would still find her unprepared.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Dalia, and why?
qa.a: Asking Thabo how he found the sources worked: she got real help with the method while the essay stayed her own.

qa.q: What is it like for Thabo when Dalia closes the folder?
qa.a: Thabo feels a little stung that his offer is turned down, but pulling up a chair suggests he accepts her choice and is willing to help in a better way.

grounding: A teenager in South Africa refuses to copy her cousin's old essay and asks him to teach her how to research instead.

passage: Study hour in the hostel reading room, and Keerthana had written four lines of her poem and crossed out three. Across the table, Chaitanya turned his tablet towards her. "Asked the chat tool for a poem about the monsoon. Look. Rhymes and everything." It was smooth, full of words like "silver" and "eternal". Keerthana's own line said the rain sounded like her mother frying mustard seeds. Beside his, it looked silly. "Do it," he whispered. "Two minutes." She typed half the request, then stopped. Ms Fernandes had said she wanted to hear "your ear, not the internet's". Keerthana deleted the words, kept the mustard seeds, and wrote six more lines about the leaking corridor roof and the warden's squeaking slippers. When the bell rang, she had a rough poem that sounded only like her.

qa.q: What did Keerthana's own line compare the rain to?
qa.a: Her mother frying mustard seeds.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she compared her line with the tablet poem?
qa.a: Keerthana felt embarrassed and tempted, because her line looked silly beside the smooth one, and she even started typing the request.

qa.q: How could Ms Fernandes support students like Keerthana when a shortcut is this easy?
qa.a: Ms Fernandes could keep praising specific personal details like the mustard seeds, so students see that their own observations are what earn credit.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see Keerthana's poem compared with his own?
qa.a: Chaitanya may think hers is rougher, but if the class responds to her real details, he might notice his borrowed poem has nothing of him in it.

grounding: A hostel student nearly asks a chat tool for a poem, then keeps her own imperfect lines because the teacher wants her voice.

passage: Last term I, Kavitha, volunteered to lead our group's stall for the science fair. Five of us, one water-filter model, three weeks. I made a chart of jobs, and when Santosh got bored cutting bottles, I sat and cut with him and let him choose the music. We were good. Then, on the morning of the fair, I insisted on moving the model myself, fast, without waiting for the trolley. The sand layer spilled across the corridor. Everyone looked at Santosh, because he had been carrying the other end. I heard myself tell Sir, "It was my call. I rushed it." My face burned. But we rebuilt a smaller version by eleven, and Santosh explained the filter to the judges better than I could have. I still remember how fast the others knelt to scoop the sand once I'd said it.

qa.q: How many people were in Kavitha's group?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when telling Sir 'It was my call'?
qa.a: Kavitha felt ashamed, with a burning face, but also determined not to let Santosh be blamed for a rushed decision.

qa.q: What worked in Kavitha's leading before the fair, and what could change next time?
qa.a: Sharing the boring work and letting Santosh pick the music kept the group going; next time Kavitha could wait for the trolley instead of rushing under pressure.

qa.q: How might Santosh see Kavitha after she owned the mistake?
qa.a: Santosh was about to be blamed, so he probably felt relieved and more loyal, which may be why he explained the filter so well to the judges.

grounding: A student leading a science fair group takes the blame for a spill she caused, and the team rallies.

passage: Advisor's note, school magazine, 3 March. Hafsa (Class 11) took over as student editor when the last one left mid-term. Nine days to print, four pages empty. She split the team by strength: Jeevan on photos, two juniors on interviews, herself on layout. When the juniors stalled, she didn't scold; she sat with them and wrote the first question together. Two days before print, the interview with the canteen staff vanished from the shared folder. Hafsa came to me first: "I moved the files and didn't tell anyone. That's on me." She then asked Jeevan to help redo it at lunch. The issue went out one day late but complete. I will suggest her for the junior leadership workshop and share the file-sharing lesson with the whole team. — Ms D'Souza, magazine advisor

qa.q: How many days were left before print when Hafsa took over?
qa.a: Nine days.

qa.q: What might Hafsa have been feeling when admitting the missing files to Ms D'Souza?
qa.a: Hafsa was probably anxious and embarrassed about the lost interview, yet responsible enough to name her own mistake before anyone else was blamed.

qa.q: How could Ms D'Souza support Hafsa's growth as a leader from here?
qa.a: Ms D'Souza could praise the honest ownership and help Hafsa set a simple rule for moving shared files, as the note already plans.

qa.q: What is it like for Jeevan to be asked to redo the interview at lunch?
qa.a: Jeevan loses a lunch break, but because Hafsa owned the mistake first, the request probably feels fair rather than like being blamed.

grounding: A teacher's note records a student editor organising the team, motivating juniors and owning a file mistake.

passage:
Saturday night
The colony cricket tournament was MY idea, so today was my fault too. I booked the ground, made the fixtures, got Amandeep's team to turn up by promising samosas at the break. Worked great till 2 pm. Then Mr Bhalla came out and said nobody had asked the society office, and we had to stop mid-match. Everyone groaned. Amandeep said, "You said it was sorted!" I wanted to say the office never replies anyway. Instead I said, "I skipped that step. Sorry, guys." Then I walked to the office with Amandeep's dad and we got Sunday afternoon approved, on paper. Felt sick the whole walk. Now I've messaged everyone the new time. Twelve thumbs up so far 👍 Maybe leading is mostly fixing.
— Kashish

qa.q: Why did the match have to stop at 2 pm?
qa.a: Nobody had asked the society office.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling on the walk to the office?
qa.a: Kashish felt sick with guilt and nervous about having let everyone down, but kept going to fix it rather than hide.

qa.q: What small step would have prevented the stoppage?
qa.a: Getting written permission from the society office before booking the ground, which is exactly what Kashish did afterwards for Sunday.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see the apology?
qa.a: Amandeep was annoyed and felt misled by 'it was sorted', but a plain apology plus an approved new time probably made the frustration easier to drop.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows organising a colony tournament, a failure from a skipped step, and owning it.

passage: On the evening bus from Kotdwar to her village, Usha finally opened her video. Twenty seconds: her Dadi's hands shaping mandua rotis, Usha's voice explaining in Garhwali, then the same line in English. Bhupen, squeezed beside her with a sack of rice, leaned over. "Garhwali? Online? The town girls will laugh." At school Usha spoke careful English and Hindi; at home, Garhwali came without thinking. For months she had kept them apart like two dupattas folded in different trunks. She looked at the comments. A stranger had written, "My nani says this word too!" Another asked what mandua was. "Let them laugh," Usha said, surprised at how steady she sounded. "Some are asking." Bhupen read the comment twice, then said quietly, "Do the next one on Dadi's pickle."

qa.q: What were Dadi's hands shaping in Usha's video?
qa.a: Mandua rotis.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she answered Bhupen?
qa.a: Usha felt a quiet pride, and some surprise at her own steadiness, after months of keeping her languages apart.

qa.q: What could help Usha keep moving between her languages without shame?
qa.a: Usha could keep pairing Garhwali with English as in the video, and pay attention to the curious comments rather than the imagined laughter.

qa.q: Why might Bhupen react differently by the end of the ride?
qa.a: The stranger recognising the word and others asking questions showed Bhupen that the language draws interest, so the teasing turned into a request for more.

grounding: A village teenager shares a video in her home language and stops hiding it from school and online worlds.

passage: At the corner table of the school cafeteria in Toronto, Rosa's phone buzzed with a voice note from her avó. She thumbed the volume down to nothing. Her avó's Portuguese was loud and warm and full of kisses, and last year someone had mimicked it for a week. Yara, unwrapping stuffed grape leaves, noticed. "You never play them." "It's embarrassing." Yara shrugged, pressed her own phone, and her teta's Arabic filled the table, asking whether Yara had eaten. A boy at the next table glanced up, then went back to his fries. "See?" Yara said. "Nobody fainted." Rosa laughed, lifted the phone to her ear and answered in Portuguese, quietly at first, then less quietly. That afternoon in English class she was the same Rosa who argued about poems. Both voices, she thought, were hers.

qa.q: In which city is Rosa's school?
qa.a: Toronto.

qa.q: Why did Rosa turn the volume down to nothing?
qa.a: Rosa felt embarrassed, because last year someone had mimicked her avó's loud Portuguese, and she feared being mocked again.

qa.q: What did Yara's example show, and how could Rosa build on it?
qa.a: Yara showed that playing a family voice note openly caused no disaster; Rosa could keep answering in Portuguese at lunch and let her confidence grow.

qa.q: How might Rosa's avó feel hearing Rosa answer from the cafeteria?
qa.a: Rosa's avó would likely feel delighted and close to Rosa, hearing Portuguese answered in the middle of a school day.

grounding: A teenager in Canada stops muting her grandmother's language at school after a friend plays her own.

passage: Heritage Day was a week away, and the hostel common room buzzed with plans. Sahil had signed up for "something funny", maybe a meme skit in the slang everyone used online. Then his mother called and sang, off-key, the Konkani boat song his grandfather used to hum while mending nets. After the call Sahil sat still, phone warm in his hand. Suraj looked down from the top bunk. "That's the song? Teach me." "It's old. People will think it's weird." "You do three accents a day, bro. English for Sir, Hindi for the mess uncle, meme voice for us. Add one." On Heritage Day Sahil sang the first verse alone, voice shaking, then Suraj joined the chorus he had practised badly all week. The juniors clapped along, and one asked Sahil to write the words down.

qa.q: Who used to hum the Konkani boat song?
qa.a: Sahil's grandfather, while mending nets.

qa.q: What might Sahil have been worried about before Heritage Day?
qa.a: Sahil was nervous that people would find the old song weird next to the easy meme skit everyone expected.

qa.q: How did Suraj help, and what could a teacher add?
qa.a: Suraj pointed out that Sahil already switches voices all day and then joined the chorus; a teacher could invite such songs through the year, not only on one day.

qa.q: How might the juniors see Sahil after the song?
qa.a: The juniors clearly enjoyed it and got curious, as one asked for the words, so Sahil probably looked brave and interesting to them.

grounding: A hostel student shares his family's Konkani song after a friend points out he already moves between many voices.

passage: Class 9 social science, project week. Kavitha chose "a family that moved" for her oral history and asked Hafsa, new this year, for an interview. Hafsa agreed only after reading the questions first. Kavitha asked why the family left their town in eastern Uttar Pradesh, what her father missed, what surprised them in Pune. In the presentation she quoted Hafsa: "On the first day, someone asked if we had electricity back home." A few students laughed. Kavitha paused, then said, "My Nani's village loses power most evenings. Nobody laughs at her." The room went quiet. Afterwards two boys asked Hafsa about her town's winter fair. I plan to make oral histories a full unit next term, and I will speak privately with the students who laughed. — Mr Pillai

qa.q: Which city did Hafsa's family move to?
qa.a: Pune.

qa.q: What does Kavitha's pause during the presentation suggest?
qa.a: Kavitha seems uncomfortable with the laughter and protective of Hafsa, choosing a calm reply from her own family's life instead of an angry one.

qa.q: What could Mr Pillai do next, beyond the plans in the note?
qa.a: Mr Pillai could let students like Hafsa choose what to share, and discuss common stereotypes openly so the laughter is understood, not just stopped.

qa.q: How might the interview have felt for Hafsa?
qa.a: Hafsa was cautious at first, but being asked real questions about home, and later about the winter fair, probably felt respectful and welcoming.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a student's curious oral history of a migrant classmate turning a prejudiced laugh into interest.

passage:
Thursday, 9:40 pm
New girl in section B, Sabina. Grew up in Nairobi, her family's Gujarati, and she speaks Swahili with her brother when she's annoyed 😅 At lunch Megha asked if she'd lived "with lions" and everyone laughed. I laughed too. Then Sabina said, flat, "We had traffic jams and a school canteen," and I wanted to vanish. So in bio I asked her real things. Why did her great-grandfather go to Kenya at all? (Railway work, about a hundred years back.) Why come back now? (Her mum's job.) What does she miss? (Mandazi, and rain on tin roofs.) I didn't know half of this history. Tomorrow I'm taking her the library book on Indian families in East Africa, and saying sorry for the lion laugh.
— Parul

qa.q: Where did Sabina grow up?
qa.a: In Nairobi.

qa.q: How did Parul feel after Sabina's flat reply about traffic jams?
qa.a: Parul felt ashamed of laughing and wanted to vanish, and that discomfort turned into curiosity about Sabina's real story.

qa.q: What small step is Parul planning, and why might it help?
qa.a: Bringing the library book and apologising for the lion laugh shows Sabina respect and keeps the curious conversation going.

qa.q: What is it like for Sabina when the table laughs about lions?
qa.a: Sabina probably feels tired and hurt at being reduced to a stereotype, which is why her reply comes out flat.

grounding: A diary shows a teenager moving from laughing at a stereotype to curious questions about a classmate's migration history.

subtype: Handling Failure, Result Disappointment & Family Crisis
passage:
"Fifty-two in maths." Parveen dropped the report card on the kitchen table. "And Abbu's shop is shut since March. Great year."
Sarita, from the flat upstairs, stopped peeling peas. "Fifty-two isn't zero."
"It's not ninety either. Ammi was counting on me."
"Did she say that?"
"No. She said, 'Eat something.' That's worse."
"What went wrong in the paper?"
"Geometry. I left the whole section."
"So it's one section, not your whole brain."
Parveen almost smiled. "You sound like a poster, Didi."
"I failed chemistry in Class 11," Sarita said. "Cried in the lift. Then I did old papers every Sunday with Anil Bhaiya. Passed with seventy."
"You never told me."
"You never failed before." Sarita pushed the bowl across. "Peel. Then we list the geometry chapters. Two a week."
Parveen took a pod, and after a moment, a pencil.

qa.q: Which section did Parveen leave in the maths paper?
qa.a: The whole geometry section.

qa.q: What does Parveen's line 'That's worse' reveal about Parveen's feelings?
qa.a: Parveen feels guilty and disappointed; Ammi's gentle reply makes Parveen sense how much the family is already carrying with Abbu's shop shut.

qa.q: Which part of Sarita's help is most useful, and why?
qa.a: Sarita shares a past failure and turns the problem into a plan of two geometry chapters a week, which shrinks the failure and gives a next step.

qa.q: How might Ammi see the fifty-two marks, given the family's situation?
qa.a: Ammi may be worried too, with the shop shut, but telling Parveen to eat suggests she cares more about her child than the number.

grounding: A teenager facing a poor result during a family money crisis is helped by a neighbour to find a hopeful plan.

subtype: Handling Failure, Result Disappointment & Family Crisis
passage: I'm Samir, and the winter my parents stopped talking to each other, I stopped doing homework. Papa slept on the sofa. Mummy spoke to him through me: "Tell your father the gas bill came." My half-yearly card came back with two reds. I hid it in my cricket bag for a week. It was Uday who found it, looking for his gloves. He didn't lecture. He said, "My parents did this in Class 7. It's not about you, but it lands on you." That sentence stuck. I asked my class teacher if I could do homework in the library after school, where it was quiet. I told Mummy the message-carrying had to stop. She cried, then agreed. Home isn't fixed. But my maths is back to a pass, and I don't dread the walk home every evening.

qa.q: Where did Samir hide the report card?
qa.a: In the cricket bag.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling during the winter the parents stopped talking?
qa.a: Samir felt stuck in the middle and ashamed of the results, hiding the card instead of asking for help.

qa.q: Which steps helped Samir, and what could a school counsellor add?
qa.a: A quiet library space and asking Mummy to stop sending messages through Samir both helped; a counsellor could offer a regular place to talk while home stays unsettled.

qa.q: How does Uday see Samir's situation?
qa.a: Uday recognises it from his own Class 7, so he sees Samir not as lazy but as someone caught in the parents' conflict.

grounding: A teenager looks back on coping with falling grades during parental conflict without losing hope.

subtype: Handling Failure, Result Disappointment & Family Crisis
passage: Counsellor's note, 14 November. Ritu (Class 12) came in after her mock results slid in three subjects. She said her mother's tailoring orders have dropped this year and the family cancelled her coaching fees; she now helps at the shop most evenings. She spoke quietly and looked tired, but said, "I still want nursing." We made a plan together: the free school revision sessions on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and Gopika, her friend, has offered to share class notes. I asked about sleep and food; she said "mostly okay". With Ritu's permission I will call her mother this week about the school's scholarship office, and I'll check in with Ritu next Friday. — S. Mehta, counsellor

qa.q: Which career does Ritu still want?
qa.a: Nursing.

qa.q: What might Ritu be feeling behind the quiet, tired manner?
qa.a: Ritu seems tired and discouraged by the slide and the family's money trouble, yet still hopeful, since nursing remains the goal.

qa.q: What made the counsellor's plan realistic for Ritu?
qa.a: It used free revision sessions, Gopika's shared notes and a scholarship contact, so Ritu could keep going without new costs, with a check-in next Friday.

qa.q: What is it like for Gopika to watch Ritu go through this?
qa.a: Gopika probably feels concerned and wants to help, so offering notes is a practical way to stand by a friend.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a student coping with poor results and family financial hardship while keeping hope.

passage: Resource room note, week 6. Gautam (Class 9) came on his own today, which is new. He said, "When I read the question paper, the lines jump. I know the answers when someone reads them out." He had tested it himself: last week Sahil read him the history questions in a free period, and he answered nine of ten aloud. We tried a ruler under each line and a larger-font sheet; he read faster and his shoulders dropped. He asked whether exam questions could be read aloud to him. I explained that he could apply through the school's support process and that we would invite his parents in. He said, "I'm not stupid. Just slow on paper." Plan: parents' meeting Thursday, a reading assessment request through the school, larger-font papers from now. — R. Nair

qa.q: How many of the history questions did Gautam answer aloud?
qa.a: Nine of ten.

qa.q: What does Gautam's line 'I'm not stupid. Just slow on paper' suggest he feels?
qa.a: He seems frustrated at being misjudged, but more confident now that he has worked out how he learns best.

qa.q: Which supports helped in the resource room, and what should come next?
qa.a: The ruler under each line and the larger-font sheet helped him read faster; next come the parents' meeting and the school's formal request, so the support is official.

qa.q: How might Sahil see his part in this?
qa.a: Sahil may feel glad and a little proud that reading the questions aloud helped Gautam discover what he needed.

grounding: A resource-room note shows a teenager noticing his own reading difficulty, testing what helps, and asking for support.

passage:
Monday
The canteen again. Plates crashing, the bell, forty people shouting over each other, and that tube light that buzzes. By half-lunch my ears ached and I snapped at Bidisha for nothing. She'd only asked if I wanted her chips 😔
Tonight I listed every time this term I've felt like this: assembly, canteen, the school bus. All loud, all bright. In quiet rooms I'm fine, better than fine: I finished the whole art project in the library in one sitting. So it's not that I'm moody. It's the noise.
Tomorrow I'll ask Ms Varghese if I can eat in the library twice a week, and wear earplugs at assembly. Scared she'll think I'm being fussy. So I've written what I'll say: "Loud rooms drain me. Quiet rooms help me work." Then I'm saying sorry to Bidisha.
— Irawati

qa.q: Where did Irawati finish the whole art project?
qa.a: In the library, in one sitting.

qa.q: What is Irawati worried about before speaking to Ms Varghese?
qa.a: Irawati is scared the teacher will think the request is fussy, even though the diary shows a clear pattern with noise.

qa.q: Why is writing down the exact sentence a good step?
qa.a: It turns the pattern into one clear request, so Irawati can ask calmly even while nervous.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt when Irawati snapped?
qa.a: Bidisha was probably hurt and puzzled, having only offered chips, so an apology and an explanation would likely mean a lot to her.

grounding: A diary shows a teenager spotting her sensitivity to noise and preparing to ask a teacher for support.

passage:
Monday. In geography, Uday copied "burning coal, petrol and gas traps heat" into his notebook and felt nothing; it was one more exam line. That evening the power went out again in the heatwave, and he lay sweating, scrolling videos of melting glaciers until he felt sick and useless.
Two weeks later. Santosh, tired of the same gloomy talk, said, "Stop doom-scrolling. What do we actually control?" They made a list on the back of a maths sheet: the scooter rides to school, the classroom fans left running, the canteen's plastic cups.
A month later. Eight students now cycled together on Wednesdays, and the prefects checked fans at every break. Uday knew it wouldn't cool the planet. But when he explained to his little sister why the air was getting hotter, he could say it without the sick feeling.

qa.q: How many students cycled together on Wednesdays a month later?
qa.a: Eight students.

qa.q: How did Uday's feelings change between the first night and a month later?
qa.a: At first Uday felt sick and useless from doom-scrolling; a month later, after small group actions, he could talk about it calmly instead of feeling hopeless.

qa.q: What made Santosh's question useful, and what could the group try next?
qa.a: It moved them from worry to what they actually control; next they could track results, like fans switched off, and share them with the school.

qa.q: How might Uday's little sister experience his explanation?
qa.a: She would probably find it easier to understand and less frightening, because Uday explains it calmly instead of passing on panic.

grounding: Over a month, a teenager moves from exam-line knowledge and climate dread to understanding and small group action.

passage: Aditi, sit, your tea will go cold. You ask why your Kalyani Paati still carries this cloth bag everywhere. Blame Mohan. Twenty years ago I taught science in Belagavi, and Mohan was the boy who argued with everything. One day he stood up and said, "Ma'am, if cars and factories are warming the earth, what can a schoolboy do? Nothing." The class laughed. I had no answer ready. That week he came back with a notebook: how many plastic bags his family used, how many scooter trips his father took that could be walked. "Not nothing," he said. "Small." He got the whole class counting. The shopkeeper near school started keeping cloth bags because thirty children kept asking. So that is how I learned it, from a boy of fifteen: knowing why it happens is half the work, and choosing what you can really do is the other half.

qa.q: What did Mohan record in his notebook?
qa.a: How many plastic bags his family used and how many scooter trips his father took that could be walked.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when the class laughed and there was no answer ready?
qa.a: Kalyani seems to have felt unsure and a little embarrassed as the teacher, which is why Mohan's notebook left such a strong mark.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Mohan's thinking, and why did it work?
qa.a: Mohan moved from 'nothing' to counting his own family's bags and trips; measuring made the problem concrete and gave the class realistic actions.

qa.q: How might the shopkeeper near the school have seen the children's requests?
qa.a: The shopkeeper probably saw real demand, with thirty children asking, and found cloth bags worth stocking, showing how small actions spread.

grounding: A grandmother tells how a fifteen-year-old student turned climate helplessness into small measurable actions.

passage: Rekha had planned a slide show. Then, on Thursday evening, the vice-principal moved the eco-club assembly to Friday morning, and the projector in the hall was still broken. Naveen stared at the laptop. "Twelve slides of graphs. Useless." Rekha pulled out the chart paper left over from Diwali decorations. "We only need three things. Why it's getting hotter. What our school wastes. What we'll do." They worked on the floor of her room until midnight: a sun over a grey blanket of smoke for the greenhouse effect, a tally of forty lights found on in empty classrooms, and a sign-up sheet for "Switch-Off Monitors". In the morning her hands shook holding the chart. But thirty-one names were on the sheet by lunch, and a Class 6 boy asked to be monitor for the whole corridor.

qa.q: How many lights did the tally show on in empty classrooms?
qa.a: Forty lights.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling as she held the chart in the morning?
qa.a: Rekha felt nervous, with shaking hands after the rushed night, but went ahead anyway.

qa.q: How did the group handle the broken projector, and why did it still work?
qa.a: They cut twelve slides down to three simple ideas on chart paper, which kept the message clear and ended with an action students could join.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel when thirty-one names appear on the sheet?
qa.a: Naveen, who thought the plan was useless without slides, would probably feel relieved and proud that the simpler version worked.

grounding: Under time pressure, a teenager explains climate causes simply and launches a realistic school energy action.

passage: Every morning at half past five, Chetan's alarm was the rooster next door. In the first week of the monsoon holidays he ran to the canal bridge and back, then gave up on the fourth day when the mud swallowed his chappal. His elder sister Sarita, home from nursing college, watched him eat three packets of chips on the verandah that afternoon. "District kabaddi trials are in two months," she said. "You want to run hard once, or a little every day?" She drew a calendar on the back of a wedding card: a short run, skipping in the yard if it rained, and a tick for every meal with dal, curd or eggs. Chetan grumbled. But the ticks started adding up. By the third week he woke before the rooster, and the chips stayed in the shop.

qa.q: What did Sarita draw the calendar on?
qa.a: The back of a wedding card.

qa.q: Why did Chetan grumble about the calendar?
qa.a: Chetan felt a bit annoyed and embarrassed at being organised by his sister after giving up, though the ticks quietly motivated him.

qa.q: What made Sarita's plan easier to keep than Chetan's first attempt?
qa.a: It had a rainy-day option and small daily ticks, so one muddy day didn't end the whole routine.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel seeing the chips stay in the shop by the third week?
qa.a: Sarita would probably feel pleased and proud that a simple, steady plan stuck instead of a burst of effort that fizzled.

grounding: A village teenager builds steady exercise and eating habits with his sister's simple daily plan.

passage: Felix used to eat a petrol-station pastry on the way to football practice in Leipzig, then wonder why his legs felt like wet socks by the second half. Abebe, the team's fastest winger, always had the same brown paper bag: a cheese sandwich, an apple, a bottle of tap water. "Boring," Felix said. "Boring works," Abebe said. "My mum says: same thing, every day, no drama." In January Felix tried it, grudgingly. He packed the night before, set the bag by the door, and added ten minutes of skipping in the courtyard before school. On rainy mornings he skipped under the stairwell. By March he hadn't magically become fast. But he stopped fading in the second half, and he noticed he felt cross on the days he forgot the bag.

qa.q: What was in Abebe's brown paper bag?
qa.a: A cheese sandwich, an apple and a bottle of tap water.

qa.q: What does Felix feeling cross on forgotten-bag days suggest?
qa.a: Felix now feels uneasy without the routine, a sign it has become a habit he values rather than a chore.

qa.q: What made the new routine stick for Felix?
qa.a: Packing the night before and having a rainy-day spot for skipping removed daily decisions, so the habit stayed consistent.

qa.q: How might Abebe see Felix's change by March?
qa.a: Abebe would probably feel quietly amused and pleased that 'boring works' turned out to be true for a teammate too.

grounding: A German teenager copies a teammate's plain, consistent food and exercise routine and sees it last.

passage: At the athletics hostel in Ranchi, the breakfast bell rang at 6:45, and most days Jyoti slept through it. She grabbed a biscuit packet on the way to the track, and by the fourth lap her legs felt like sandbags. Coach Ekka noticed her slowing and waved her to the bench. "What did you eat?" "Biscuits." "That's not fuel. And you're on your phone till midnight, aren't you?" Jyoti looked down at her spikes. Her roommate Bidisha, who never missed breakfast, offered a deal: phones in the locker at ten, and she would shake Jyoti awake for the bell. The first week was miserable. By the second, Jyoti was eating poha and a banana before training and finishing her laps strong. She wrote "10 pm" on the mirror in eyeliner so she wouldn't forget.

qa.q: What time did the breakfast bell ring?
What does Jyoti looking down at her spikes suggest?
qa.a: Jyoti seems embarrassed and a bit guilty, knowing the coach is right about the late nights and biscuit breakfasts.

qa.q: Which part of the deal made the change last?
qa.a: Locking phones away at ten fixed the real cause, late nights, and Bidisha's wake-up made breakfast easy to reach; the mirror note kept it going.

qa.q: What is it like for Bidisha to take on the wake-up job?
qa.a: Bidisha probably finds it a small effort worth making, and may feel glad to see her roommate running strongly.

grounding: At a sports hostel, a teenager fixes her sleep and breakfast habits with a roommate's help.

passage:
Wednesday
Philosophy club today. Mr Dsouza gave us the old question about lying to protect a friend. Half of us said a lie that saves someone is fine because the result is good. The other half said lying is wrong, full stop. I switched sides twice.
At dinner I asked Nazia Apa. She said our faith teaches honesty as a duty, but also mercy, so maybe it isn't either-or. Then Abbu brought up Mahavir Uncle, his friend from the office, who is Jain and tries to choose whatever causes the least harm, even to insects.
What I noticed: nobody at that table was stupid. Each view protects something: results, rules, mercy, not harming. My job isn't to pick a team by Friday. It's to ask what each side is protecting.
— Farhan

qa.q: What question did Mr Dsouza give the philosophy club?
qa.a: The old question about lying to protect a friend.

qa.q: What does switching sides twice suggest about Farhan's state of mind?
qa.a: Farhan felt genuinely torn, seeing sense both in judging by results and in keeping to rules.

qa.q: What is useful about Farhan's question of what each side is protecting?
qa.a: It lets Farhan compare the views fairly, finding the value in each instead of dismissing any as stupid.

qa.q: How might Nazia Apa see Farhan's questions at dinner?
qa.a: Nazia Apa seems glad to be asked, sharing that honesty and mercy both matter in their faith, and may enjoy thinking it through together.

grounding: A teenager's diary compares result-based, rule-based, faith-based and non-harming views of an ethical question fairly.

passage: At the tea stall on the Pandharpur road, Yamini's Aaji hummed abhangs while frying bhaji, and Bhavna from the next lane sat on the bench reading about the Buddha for a school essay. That week a street play came through the kasba, actors in black shirts shouting that every miracle was a trick. Aaji tutted. Bhavna frowned. Yamini, the only one without a strong opinion, felt pulled three ways. That night she wrote in her rough book: Aaji's faith makes her kind to every pilgrim who stops. Bhavna's teaching says test everything against your own experience. The actors wanted proof. Under each she added two questions: What does this give people? Where could it go wrong? Next morning she asked Aaji and Bhavna the same two questions, and neither of them got angry.

qa.q: What did the actors in the street play claim?
qa.a: That every miracle was a trick.

qa.q: Why did Yamini feel pulled three ways?
qa.a: Yamini respected Aaji's faith, Bhavna's questioning and the actors' demand for proof, so she felt torn and unsure without a strong opinion of her own.

qa.q: Why did asking the same two questions to Aaji and Bhavna work?
qa.a: The questions were fair to every view, asking what it gives and where it could go wrong, so nobody felt attacked.

qa.q: How might Aaji have felt watching the street play?
qa.a: Aaji tutted, so she likely felt offended or dismissive, since the play mocked the kind of devotion she lives by.

grounding: In a small town, a teenager compares her grandmother's devotion, a friend's Buddhist teaching and rationalist actors with fair questions.

passage:
"Month three," Pradeep groaned, flopping onto the divan with the harmonium book. "Same scales. Same raag. Every. Single. Day."
His mother Usha looked up from the accounts. "You said you wanted to play at Didi's wedding."
"In December. It's August. That's forever."
"Remember the first week? You couldn't even find Sa."
"That was different. That was exciting."
"And now it's boring because you're past the exciting part." She tapped the calendar. "Twelve songs by December. How many can you play?"
Pradeep counted on his fingers. "Four. Four and a half."
"In three months. So?"
"Eight more in four months." He sat up slowly. "If I learn one every two weeks."
"And on boring days?"
"Fifteen minutes only. Not an hour."
"Deal. And Pradeep, Didi will cry either way."
He laughed and pulled the harmonium closer.

qa.q: How many songs did Pradeep need to play by December?
qa.a: Twelve songs.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he flopped onto the divan?
qa.a: Pradeep felt bored and fed up with repeating the same scales, and December seemed impossibly far away.

qa.q: What made the new plan more likely to survive boring days?
qa.a: Breaking the goal into one song every two weeks and allowing just fifteen minutes on dull days kept the target small and steady.

qa.q: How does Usha see Pradeep's boredom?
qa.a: Usha sees it as a normal stage after the exciting start, so she calmly helps him count his progress instead of scolding.

grounding: A teenager bored three months into learning harmonium works out a steady plan with his mother to reach a December goal.

passage: Last year I, Gurleen, promised to finish one phulkari dupatta by my Biji's seventieth birthday. Seven months, one dupatta, thousands of stitches. The first month I stitched every evening and posted progress photos. By month three I hated the colour orange. Some nights I did four stitches and put it away. My friend Ishita, training for the district swim meet, told me her coach's rule: never skip two days in a row. So on bad days I did one line, just one, and ticked it in a notebook. Once I knocked chai over it and a stain spread across a corner. I cried for an hour, then stitched a flower over it. On her birthday Biji found that flower first and asked about it. I told her the whole story.

qa.q: What was Ishita training for?
qa.a: The district swim meet.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling after the chai stain spread across the corner?
qa.a: Gurleen was heartbroken and cried for an hour, then felt determined enough to turn the stain into a flower.

qa.q: Which rule helped on the boring days, and why?
qa.a: Never skipping two days in a row, even with one line, kept the habit alive when the project felt dull.

qa.q: What might it be like for Biji to find the flower first?
qa.a: Biji would probably feel touched and curious, and hearing about the stain may make the dupatta mean even more to her.

grounding: A teenager looks back on sustaining a seven-month embroidery project through boredom and a setback.

passage: Mentor's log, robotics lab, week 19 of 26. Lavanya's solar model car has now failed its test run three times. In week 12 the motor burnt out, and she waited two weeks for a new one. Harish, her teammate, stopped coming for most of that month; he told me, "It's the same wiring every day, sir. I'm bored stiff." Lavanya kept a paper chart on the wall: one small target per session, a line through each finished one. Today she asked whether she should cut the lights from the design to finish on time. I asked what the car must do by week 26. She decided: drive ten metres in sunlight, nothing more. Harish came back once she handed him the steering to redesign as his own piece. Next, I'll ask both to present the chart at the club meeting. — Mr Kulkarni

qa.q: In which week did the motor burn out?
qa.a: Week 12.

qa.q: What might Lavanya have been feeling when asking whether to cut the lights?
qa.a: Lavanya was probably worried about finishing on time after three failed runs, yet still determined, looking to simplify rather than quit.

qa.q: What habit kept Lavanya going, and what did Mr Kulkarni add?
qa.a: The wall chart of one small target per session; Mr Kulkarni's question about what the car truly needs helped her trim the goal.

qa.q: How might Harish see the project once the steering is his own?
qa.a: Owning a piece gives Harish something new to solve instead of the same wiring, so it likely feels interesting and worth the effort again.

grounding: A mentor's log shows a teenager sustaining a six-month robotics project through setbacks and a bored teammate.
